prompt: What does the lesson mean by shadow storage?
hint: Who chose the service, and with whose e-mail was it opened?

choices.text: Company data in somebody's own account
choices.why: Right. The company has no administrator in it and no contract with the provider.

choices.text: A backup copy the provider keeps without telling the customer
choices.why: That is not a thing the lesson describes; the copies it worries about are made by people.

choices.text: A bucket in a region of the account that nobody looks at
choices.why: That is a forgotten resource inside the company's own account, the subject of lesson 1's inventory loop.

choices.text: Encrypted storage whose key was lost
choices.why: Nothing to do with keys; it is about where a copy lives and who controls it.

prompt: bia uploaded the spreadsheet to her personal Drive to help the accountant. Of the losses in the lesson's table, which one does it call the one that matters most?
hint: Every defence starts from it.

choices.text: The accountant may forward the link
choices.why: A real risk, but the table's last row is the one the lesson singles out.

choices.text: The file is outside every inventory the clinic has
choices.why: Right. Nobody can protect, audit or delete what nobody knows about.

choices.text: Google charges the clinic for the storage the spreadsheet takes up in bia's account
choices.why: Google bills bia's account, if anyone; the clinic is not involved at all, which is the problem.

choices.text: bia broke a written rule, and has to be disciplined for it
choices.why: The lesson says she broke no rule she knew about; she was being helpful.

prompt: A copy of patients' appointments sits in a former employee's personal Dropbox. Under the LGPD, as the lesson puts it, whose responsibility is that data?
hint: The controller does not stop being the controller when a copy moves.

choices.text: Dropbox's, since the data is on its servers
choices.why: Dropbox has no relationship with the clinic at all; the copy is in a personal account.

choices.text: Nobody's any more, because the employee left
choices.why: Leaving the job does not end the clinic's duty over its patients' data.

choices.text: Still the clinic's, wherever the copy is
choices.why: Right. The clinic remains the controller wherever a copy ends up.

choices.text: The former employee's alone, as the person who made the copy
choices.why: She may answer for it too, but the clinic remains the controller of its patients' data.

prompt: Match each way shadow storage happens to an example.
hint: The three ways at the end of the first section.

pairs.left: a personal account used for work
pairs.right: bia's own Google Drive, opened with her home address

pairs.left: a company account shared too widely
pairs.right: a file in the clinic's Workspace shared with anyone with the link

pairs.left: company storage handed out by link
pairs.right: a presigned URL to an object in the clinic's bucket

right_distractors: a bucket policy granting the principal `*`

prompt: Why does the lesson call an open link a key written as an address?
hint: What does a person need to open the file?

choices.text: Because the address is encrypted with the owner's key
choices.why: Nothing about the address is encrypted; holding it is enough.

choices.text: Whoever holds the address holds the file
choices.why: Right. It is a bearer credential that people copy without thinking of it as one.

choices.text: Because opening it asks for a password that is part of the address
choices.why: An open link asks for nothing at all.

choices.text: Because each link can be used once, like a door key handed back after use
choices.why: Open links work as often as anybody likes, for as long as they live.

prompt: A colleague says an open link is safe because its address is long and random, so nobody can guess it. What does the lesson answer?
hint: Guessing is not how the address travels.

choices.text: That is right, as long as it is never posted on a public page
choices.why: It does not need to be posted: everyone it was given to, and everyone they give it to, can open it.

choices.text: Guessing is not the risk; everybody it reaches is, for as long as it works
choices.why: Right. A link sent in March still opens the file in October, from somebody else's laptop.

choices.text: Long addresses are guessed easily by modern computers
choices.why: The lesson agrees guessing is not the risk; the risk is the people it is handed to.

choices.text: It is safe only if the service also logs who opened it, with a name
choices.why: An open link is exactly the case where the log cannot name anybody.

prompt: The clinic's administrator turns off sharing outside the organisation in the clinic's Google Workspace. What does that change for bia's personal Google Drive?
hint: Read the last column of the table.

choices.text: Nothing: it is a separate account that setting never reaches
choices.why: Right. Every administrator control belongs to the company's own tenant.

choices.text: Her open links stop working, since both are Google Drive
choices.why: Same product, different account; the clinic's setting does not reach it.

choices.text: Her files move into the clinic's Workspace
choices.why: No setting moves files between unrelated accounts.

choices.text: Her account is suspended until she signs in with her work address
choices.why: The clinic has no power over a personal account at all.

prompt: Which of these does the lesson ask of any shared link? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two questions, and a third for whoever defends.

choices.text: Who can open it
choices.why: Right: named people, the organisation, or anybody.

choices.text: Until when it works
choices.why: Right: a date, or never.

choices.text: Whether the defender can see it exists, and take it back
choices.why: Right. On a company account, yes; on a personal one, the company is not asked.

choices.text: How long the address is
choices.why: Length protects against guessing, which is not the risk.

choices.text: Which browser it was created in
choices.why: Irrelevant to who can open it.

prompt: What sends `aws s3 presign` to AWS when it makes a link?
hint: The signature is arithmetic.

choices.text: A request to register the link, so the bucket can list it later
choices.why: There is no list of links anywhere; that is why revoking one means acting on the key.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right. It signs locally with the key in your environment, the object's name and the time.

choices.text: The secret key, so AWS can check the signature
choices.why: The secret key never leaves; AWS recomputes the signature with its own copy when the link is used.

choices.text: The object itself, to make a public copy of it
choices.why: No copy is made; the link reads the private object directly.

prompt: Which part of a presigned URL tells a defender whose key is handing a file out?
hint: On AWS it starts with AKIA for a user's key.

choices.text: `X-Amz-Signature`
choices.why: The signature proves the key, but it does not name it.

choices.text: `X-Amz-SignedHeaders`
choices.why: That lists what else the signature covers.

choices.text: `X-Amz-Credential`
choices.why: Right. It carries the access key id, with date, region and service.

choices.text: `X-Amz-Algorithm`
choices.why: That says how it was signed.

prompt: A presigned URL carries `X-Amz-Expires=900`. For how many minutes after `X-Amz-Date` does AWS honour it?
hint: The value is in seconds.

prompt: In the lab, a link made to last ten seconds was used fifteen seconds later and moto served the file. What would AWS have done?
hint: moto checks neither the expiry nor the signature.

choices.text: Served it too, since the signature on the address was still valid and untouched
choices.why: A valid signature on an expired link is still refused.

choices.text: Refused it with `403`, `AccessDenied`, *Request has expired*
choices.why: Right, from AWS's documentation; not run here, because moto serves it.

choices.text: Served it with a warning header, then deleted the link from the bucket's list
choices.why: There is no list of links in a bucket, and an expired link is refused, not warned about.

choices.text: Refused it with `SignatureDoesNotMatch`
choices.why: That is the answer to an address whose signature was altered; this one is intact and late.

prompt: caio signed fifty result links last week with his own IAM user's key, and one went to the wrong patient. What takes that link back?
hint: A link carries the signer's permissions at the moment it is used.

choices.text: Deleting the link from the bucket's list of shared links
choices.why: There is no such list; nothing about a link is stored in the bucket.

choices.text: Deactivating caio's key, which also kills the other forty-nine
choices.why: Right, and it is why the lesson wants a dedicated signing role rather than a person's own key.

choices.text: Nothing: it lives until its expiry
choices.why: Removing the signer's key or permission ends it at once.

choices.text: Renaming the object, then asking the patient to delete the e-mail
choices.why: Renaming works for that one object only by accident and breaks the right links too; the lesson's answer is the key.

prompt: Why does the lesson prefer links signed from a role session over links signed with a user's key?
hint: Temporary credentials have an end.

choices.text: A role's links are encrypted and a user's are not
choices.why: Both are signed the same way; neither encrypts the address.

choices.text: Links from a role session can be listed and deleted from the console, unlike the others
choices.why: No link of any kind is listed anywhere.

choices.text: They die when the session does, whatever `--expires-in` said
choices.why: Right. A one-hour session makes links that stop within the hour.

prompt: Of the three things a company controls, which does the lesson say matters most against shadow storage?
hint: A rule without an alternative moves the file somewhere the rule cannot see.

choices.text: A firewall rule blocking every storage service
choices.why: Blocking the service also blocks the company's own tenant, and phones on mobile data pass anyway.

choices.text: A company service as easy as people's own, with sharing set narrowly
choices.why: Right. Give people the quick way, configured the way the company wants.

choices.text: A written policy forbidding personal accounts
choices.why: Without an equally easy company service, the file just moves out of sight.

choices.text: Asking people to delete copies when they leave
choices.why: That is the last resort the lesson ends on, not the first defence.

prompt: Why can't the clinic simply block `drive.google.com` to keep files out of personal Drives?
hint: Tenant restrictions check something other than the address.

choices.text: The company's own Drive uses the same address
choices.why: Right. What has to be checked is which account is signing in.

choices.text: Because blocking an address is against the LGPD
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says so; the problem is technical.

choices.text: Google encrypts the address, so a firewall cannot read it
choices.why: The lesson's reason is that the company uses the same address.

choices.text: Google forbids companies from blocking it
choices.why: No such prohibition is mentioned.

prompt: What does a CASB give a company, in the lesson's words?
hint: It reads logs the company already has.

choices.text: An encrypted copy of every file anybody uploads to a personal account, kept for audits
choices.why: It lists services and volumes; it keeps no copies.

choices.text: A list of the cloud services people use, and how much each receives
choices.why: Right. It is how shadow storage is found in the first place.

choices.text: Administrator access to employees' personal accounts
choices.why: Nothing gives a company that; the account is not the company's.

choices.text: A way to delete files from personal Dropbox accounts
choices.why: No control reaches into an account the company does not own.

prompt: A request signed in the address, as a presigned URL is, carries `s3:authType` equal to `___`.
hint: Three words in capitals, joined by hyphens.

prompt: caio makes result links with `--expires-in 86400`. The bucket policy denies `s3:GetObject` when `s3:signatureAge` is greater than `600000`. On AWS, how long does one of caio's links work?
hint: The unit of `s3:signatureAge`, and which promise wins.

choices.text: A day, because the signer chose it
choices.why: The signer's expiry is a promise; the bucket's `Deny` is a guardrail and ends it sooner.

choices.text: Ten minutes, because 600,000 milliseconds is ten minutes and an explicit Deny beats it
choices.why: Right. Not run here: moto ignores conditions.

choices.text: Six hundred seconds short of a day
choices.why: The condition does not subtract; it refuses any signature older than its limit.

choices.text: It never works, because the policy denies every presigned request
choices.why: That would be the `s3:authType` policy, which the lesson put on `clinic-records`.

prompt: Why does the lesson say shadow storage is the one exposure whose fix cannot be proved by asking again?
hint: Where would the clinic send the anonymous request?

choices.text: Because personal providers refuse anonymous requests
choices.why: Some links answer anybody; the issue is that the clinic does not know where they are.

choices.text: The clinic has nowhere to ask: it does not know where the copies are
choices.why: Right. That is why every control in the lesson prevents rather than cleans up.

choices.text: Because the LGPD forbids testing someone else's account
choices.why: Not the lesson's reason.

choices.text: Asking again only works on AWS, and these files are on other providers' servers, out of the lab's reach
choices.why: Asking works against any address; the problem is not knowing the address at all.

prompt: Put the steps of the presigned-URL experiment in the order the section ran them.
hint: Prove the bucket private before handing anything out.
items: upload the result to a new bucket
ask for it anonymously and get 403
sign a link that lasts fifteen minutes
open the link with no credentials and read the file
sign a ten-second link, wait, and watch moto still serve it
trap: Putting the anonymous 403 after the link is the slip: it is the proof the link is the only way in.

prompt: Match each service to its open link, as the lesson's table names it.
hint: The second column of the table.

pairs.right: *Anyone with the link*, with no company administrator
